notes.front: What is an issue on GitHub?
notes.back: An item you create in a repository to plan, discuss and track work, such as a bug report or a new feature idea.
notes.explanation: The docs describe issues as quick to create and flexible, so one tool can be used in many ways.
notes.example: Like a ticket on a shared to-do board, but kept alongside the repository it concerns.
notes.evidence: You can create issues in your repository to plan, discuss, and track work. Issues are quick to create, flexible, and can be used in many ways. Issues can track bug reports, new features and ideas

notes.front: What is a sub-issue?
notes.back: An issue added under another issue, to break a larger piece of work into smaller issues.
notes.explanation: Sub-issues create relationships between issues, so work forms a hierarchy, and it can go several levels deep.
notes.example: Like chapters under a book project: each tracked on its own, but still part of the book.
notes.evidence: You can add sub-issues to an issue to quickly break down larger pieces of work into smaller issues. Sub-issues add support for hierarchies of issues on GitHub by creating relationships between your issues. You can create multiple levels of sub-issues

notes.front: What is an issue dependency?
notes.back: A blocking relationship between issues, showing which issues are blocked by, or are blocking, other work.
notes.explanation: It records which work must wait for other work, rather than which work is part of a larger piece.
notes.example: Like “paint the walls” waiting on “fix the plaster”: one job cannot start until the other is done.
notes.evidence: You can define blocking relationships between issues using issue dependencies. Issue dependencies let you identify issues that are blocked by, or blocking, other work.

notes.front: What is a pull request (PR)?
notes.back: A pull request (PR) is a proposal to merge code changes into a project, so people can discuss and review them before merging.
notes.explanation: The docs call it GitHub’s key collaboration feature: it helps teams work together, catch issues early and maintain code quality.
notes.example: Like handing an editor a marked-up draft: nothing goes into the book until the changes are discussed and accepted.
notes.evidence: Pull requests are proposals to merge code changes into a project. A pull request is GitHub's key **collaboration feature**, letting you discuss and review changes before merging them. This helps teams work together, catch issues early, and maintain code quality.

notes.front: What is a draft pull request?
notes.back: A pull request marked as a draft: it cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically asked to review it.
notes.explanation: Drafts suit sharing work in progress without formally requesting reviews.
notes.example: Like circulating a report stamped “draft, not for sign-off”.
notes.evidence: When you create a pull request, you can choose to make it a draft pull request. Draft pull requests cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically requested to review them. Drafts are useful when you want to share work-in-progress without formally requesting reviews.

notes.front: What is GitHub Discussions?
notes.back: A place for a project’s community to hold open-ended conversations about the project’s direction and future, without third-party tools.
notes.explanation: Maintainers, contributors and visitors all gather in one central location on GitHub.
notes.example: Like a community forum attached to the project, rather than its to-do list.
notes.evidence: GitHub Discussions allows your project's community to engage in conversations about the project's direction and future in an open-ended format. Maintainers, contributors, and visitors can gather in a central location, without third-party tools.

notes.front: What is a closing keyword?
notes.back: A supported word, such as closes, fixes or resolves, in a pull request description or commit message that links the pull request to an issue.
notes.explanation: The keyword only takes effect when the pull request targets the repository's default branch.
notes.example: Writing “Fixes #12” in a pull request that repairs the bug reported in issue 12.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “Linking a pull request to an issue using a keyword”
notes.evidence: You can link a pull request to an issue by using a supported keyword in the pull request's description or in a commit message. The pull request **must be** on the default branch.

notes.front: What is an issue template?
notes.back: A ready-made starting point that contributors select when opening a new issue in a repository.
notes.explanation: Templates can be built with the issue template builder or with issue forms.
notes.example: Like a help-desk “bug report” sheet with headings for what you did, what you expected and what happened.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Issue templates”
notes.evidence: When you create issue templates for your repository using the issue template builder or with issue forms, contributors can select the appropriate template when they open new issues in the repository.

notes.front: What is a pull request template?
notes.back: Content added to a repository that contributors automatically see in the body of a new pull request.
notes.explanation: Contributors start their description from the template’s contents instead of a blank box.
notes.example: Like a checklist printed at the top of every change request form.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Pull request templates”
notes.evidence: When you add a pull request template to your repository, project contributors will automatically see the template's contents in the pull request body.

notes.front: What is a notification on GitHub?
notes.back: An update about activity on GitHub that you have subscribed to.
notes.explanation: You customise, triage and manage these updates in the notifications inbox.
notes.example: Like a doorbell that rings only for the parcels you signed up to receive.
notes.evidence: Notifications provide updates about the activity on GitHub that you've subscribed to. You can use the notifications inbox to customize, triage, and manage your updates.

notes.front: What is a subscription, in GitHub notifications?
notes.back: Your choice to receive ongoing updates about specific activity, such as one issue’s conversation or all activity in a repository.
notes.explanation: The subscription decides what you hear about; notifications are the updates it produces.
notes.example: Like following one topic in a news app rather than every story it publishes.
notes.evidence: You can choose to receive ongoing updates about specific activity on GitHub through a subscription. Notifications are updates that you receive for specific activity that you are subscribed to.

notes.front: What is a gist?
notes.back: A simple way to share code snippets with others. Every gist is a Git repository, so it can be cloned.
notes.explanation: Underneath the simple snippet is a full Git repository, which is what makes cloning possible.
notes.example: Like posting a single recipe card rather than publishing the whole cookbook.
notes.evidence: Gists provide a simple way to share code snippets with others. Every gist is a Git repository, which means that it can be forked and cloned.

notes.front: What is a wiki in a GitHub repository?
notes.back: A section of the repository for long-form documentation, such as how to use the project or how it was designed.
notes.explanation: A README quickly says what a project can do; the wiki holds the additional documentation.
notes.example: Like the full manual that sits behind a product’s one-page quick-start card.
notes.evidence: You can use your repository's wiki to share long-form content about your project, such as how to use it, how you designed it, or its core principles. A README file quickly tells what your project can do, while you can use a wiki to provide additional documentation.

notes.front: What is GitHub Pages?
notes.back: A static site hosting service that publishes a website from the `.html`, `.css` and JavaScript files in a GitHub repository.
notes.explanation: It can optionally run the files through a build process before publishing the site.
notes.example: Like a shop window that displays whatever pages you place in one particular folder.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub Pages?”, “About GitHub Pages”
notes.evidence: GitHub Pages is a static site hosting service that takes HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files straight from a repository on GitHub, optionally runs the files through a build process, and publishes a website.

notes.front: A team’s “rebuild the checkout page” issue is too large to track as one item. They want each smaller task tracked as its own issue, grouped under the big one. What should they use?
notes.back: C) Sub-issues.
notes.choices:
A) A closing keyword
B) An issue dependency
C) Sub-issues
notes.choicesExplained: B records that one issue blocks another, not that it is part of it. C links a pull request to an issue.
notes.explanation: Sub-issues break larger pieces of work into smaller issues and build a hierarchy between them.
notes.evidence: You can add sub-issues to an issue to quickly break down larger pieces of work into smaller issues.

notes.front: Issue A, “publish the release notes”, cannot start until issue B, “fix the login flaw”, is finished. How do you record that on GitHub?
notes.back: A) Add an issue dependency, marking A as blocked by B.
notes.choices:
A) Add an issue dependency: A is blocked by B
B) Make A a sub-issue of B
C) Mention B in A’s description
notes.choicesExplained: A says A is part of A, not that it must wait for A. C only creates a reference between them.
notes.explanation: Issue dependencies define blocking relationships, showing which issues are blocked by other work.
notes.evidence: You can define blocking relationships between issues using issue dependencies. Issue dependencies let you identify issues that are blocked by, or blocking, other work.

notes.front: Which pull request tab shows the description, timeline, comments and reviews?
notes.back: The Conversation tab.
notes.explanation: The tabs organise the context reviewers need to understand a change, and this one holds the discussion.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Pull requests”, “Working with pull requests”
notes.evidence: A pull request brings together the context reviewers need to understand a change. This context is organized into tabs: * The **Conversation** tab shows the description, timeline, comments, and reviews.

notes.front: Which pull request tab shows the diff that reviewers use to understand the proposed changes?
notes.back: The Files changed tab.
notes.explanation: Other tabs hold discussion, history and automated results; this one shows the change itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Pull requests”, “Working with pull requests”
notes.evidence: The **Files changed** tab shows the diff that reviewers use to understand the proposed changes.

notes.front: What does a pull request’s Checks tab show?
notes.back: Automated tests, builds and other validations.
notes.explanation: These are automated results, kept apart from the human comments and reviews on the Conversation tab.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Pull requests”, “Working with pull requests”
notes.evidence: The **Checks** tab shows automated tests, builds, and other validations.

notes.front: What happens when you mark a draft pull request as ready for review?
notes.back: Reviews are requested from any code owners.
notes.explanation: While it is a draft, code owners are not asked automatically; marking it ready is the point where they are.
notes.evidence: When you're ready to get feedback on your pull request, you can mark your draft pull request as ready for review. Marking a pull request as ready for review will request reviews from any code owners. You can convert a pull request to a draft at any time.

notes.front: You have pushed half-finished code and want teammates to see it early. It must not be merged by accident, and code owners should not be asked to review yet. What do you open?
notes.back: A) A draft pull request.
notes.choices:
A) A draft pull request
B) An issue describing the code
C) An ordinary pull request
notes.choicesExplained: B: an issue carries no code changes to review. C: an ordinary pull request can be merged.
notes.explanation: Drafts cannot be merged, do not automatically request code owners, and are meant for sharing work in progress.
notes.evidence: Draft pull requests cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically requested to review them. Drafts are useful when you want to share work-in-progress without formally requesting reviews.

notes.front: What are two things a community can do in GitHub Discussions?
notes.back: For example, share announcements and gauge community opinion with polls (among others).
notes.explanation: The docs also list planning decisions with community input and answering questions, which can be marked as answered.
notes.evidence: Share announcements and information * Plan and make decisions with community input * Encourage and answer questions, and mark them answered as you respond to them * Gauge community opinion using polls

notes.front: What must happen before anyone can use GitHub Discussions in a repository or organization?
notes.back: An administrator must enable GitHub Discussions for it.
notes.explanation: Once it is enabled, anyone with access to the repository or organization can create and join discussions.
notes.evidence: Anyone with access to a repository or organization can create and participate in discussions there. However, an administrator must enable GitHub Discussions for the repository or organization first.

notes.front: Repository discussions versus organization discussions: what is each for?
notes.back: Repository discussions: topics specific to one repository. Organization discussions: broader conversations that span several repositories.
notes.explanation: The choice follows the scope of the conversation.
notes.evidence: You can use **repository** discussions to discuss topics that are specific to one repository and **organization** discussions for broader conversations that span multiple repositories.

notes.front: Which kinds of conversation does GitHub suggest are more suitable for Discussions than for issues?
notes.back: Asking and answering questions, sharing information, making announcements, and general conversation about a project.
notes.explanation: Issues are for planning and tracking work; these open-ended exchanges fit Discussions better.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issues”, “Comparing issues and discussions”
notes.evidence: Some conversations are more suitable for GitHub Discussions. You can use GitHub Discussions to ask and answer questions, share information, make announcements, and conduct or participate in conversations about a project.

notes.front: Which of these belongs in an issue rather than in GitHub Discussions?
notes.back: A) The bug report.
notes.choices:
A) A bug report with the steps that trigger it
B) A poll on which feature to build next year
C) A newcomer asking how to get started
notes.choicesExplained: B gauges community opinion and C is a question to answer: both are what Discussions are for.
notes.explanation: Issues exist to track work, and bug reports are the first thing the docs list.
notes.evidence: Issues can track bug reports, new features and ideas, and anything else you need to write down or discuss with your team

notes.front: Which three words, in their different forms, are GitHub’s closing keywords?
notes.back: Close, fix and resolve (for example closes, fixed, resolves).
notes.explanation: Each word is supported in three forms, making nine keywords in all.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “Linking a pull request to an issue using a keyword”
notes.evidence: close closes closed fix fixes fixed resolve resolves resolved

notes.front: What syntax links a pull request to an issue in the same repository?
notes.back: `KEYWORD #ISSUE-NUMBER`, for example `Resolves #7`.
notes.explanation: Within one repository the issue number alone is enough.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “Linking a pull request to an issue using a keyword”
notes.evidence: Issue in the same repository | KEYWORD #ISSUE-NUMBER

notes.front: What syntax links a pull request to an issue in a different repository?
notes.back: `KEYWORD OWNER/REPOSITORY#ISSUE-NUMBER`, for example `Fixes my-team/tools#42`.
notes.explanation: The owner and repository name tell GitHub which repository’s issue number is meant.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “Linking a pull request to an issue using a keyword”
notes.evidence: Issue in a different repository | KEYWORD OWNER/REPOSITORY#ISSUE-NUMBER

notes.front: Closing keywords in a pull request description work only when the pull request targets which branch?
notes.back: The repository’s default branch.
notes.explanation: If it targets any other branch, the keywords are ignored, no links are created, and merging has no effect on the issues.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “About linked issues and pull requests”
notes.evidence: The special keywords in a pull request description are interpreted only when the pull request targets the repository's *default* branch. If the pull request targets *any other branch*, then these keywords are ignored, no links are created, and merging the PR has no effect on the issues.

notes.front: A pull request into a “staging” branch (not the default branch) says “Resolves #30” in its description. It is merged. What happens to issue 30?
notes.back: C) It stays open, and no link was made.
notes.choices:
A) It is closed automatically
B) It is linked, but stays open until someone closes it
C) It stays open, and no link was ever made
notes.choicesExplained: A: keywords count only when the pull request targets the default branch. B: against another branch, no links are created at all.
notes.explanation: Against any branch other than the default, keywords are ignored and merging has no effect on the issues.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “About linked issues and pull requests”
notes.evidence: If the pull request targets *any other branch*, then these keywords are ignored, no links are created, and merging the PR has no effect on the issues.

notes.front: Who can link issues to a pull request manually from its sidebar, and how many issues?
notes.back: Anyone with write permissions to the repository; up to ten issues per pull request, in the same repository.
notes.explanation: This is the alternative to closing keywords, and it does not depend on the pull request’s description.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Linking a pull request to an issue”, “Manually linking a pull request to an issue using the pull request sidebar”
notes.evidence: Anyone with write permissions to a repository can manually link a pull request to an issue from the pull request sidebar. You can manually link up to ten issues to each pull request. The issue and pull request must be in the same repository.

notes.front: Where are issue templates stored?
notes.back: On the repository’s default branch, in the hidden .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE directory.
notes.explanation: A template created in another branch is not available for collaborators to use.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Issue templates”
notes.evidence: Issue templates are stored on the repository's default branch, in a hidden `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE` directory. If you create a template in another branch, it will not be available for collaborators to use.

notes.front: A maintainer needs contributors to give specific, structured information in every issue. Issue template or issue form?
notes.back: An issue form, which uses web form fields; a plain template guides contributors but lets them write their own content.
notes.explanation: Forms help ensure you receive the information you want; templates offer guidance while leaving the content open.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Issue templates”
notes.evidence: Issue templates are helpful when you want to provide guidance for opening issues while allowing contributors to specify the content of their issues. If you want contributors to provide specific, structured information when they open issues, issue forms help ensure that you receive your desired information.

notes.front: Where in a repository can you store a pull request template?
notes.back: The visible root directory, the docs folder or the hidden .github directory, on the default branch.
notes.explanation: Any of the three places works, as long as the template is on the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Pull request templates”
notes.evidence: You can store your pull request template in the repository's visible root directory, the `docs` folder, or the hidden `.github` directory.

notes.front: A maintainer commits a new pull request template to a feature branch. Contributors opening pull requests never see it. What is wrong?
notes.back: A) Templates must be created on the default branch.
notes.choices:
A) The template is not on the default branch
B) Templates only work in organizations
C) The filename must be in capitals
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing limits templates to organizations. C: pull request template filenames are not case sensitive.
notes.explanation: Templates created in other branches are not available for collaborators to use.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About issue and pull request templates”, “Pull request templates”
notes.evidence: You must create templates on the repository's default branch. Templates created in other branches are not available for collaborators to use. You can store your pull request template in the repository's visible root directory, the `docs` folder, or the hidden `.github` directory. Pull request template filenames are not case sensitive

notes.front: What are two of the default filters for issues and pull requests?
notes.back: For example, items you have created and items assigned to you (among others).
notes.explanation: The list also includes all open items and items where you are @mentioned.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Filtering and searching issues and pull requests”, “Filtering issues and pull requests”
notes.evidence: All open issues and pull requests * Issues and pull requests that you've created * Issues and pull requests that are assigned to you * Issues and pull requests where you're **@mentioned**

notes.front: In an advanced issue filter, how does GitHub treat a space between two statements that have no `AND` or `OR`?
notes.back: As an `AND` operator.
notes.explanation: Leaving out the operators is allowed; the space quietly takes the place of `AND`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Filtering and searching issues and pull requests”, “Using boolean operators”
notes.evidence: If you choose not to use `AND` and `OR` operators, GitHub will treat a space between statements as an `AND` operator.

notes.front: You want to see issues assigned to either the user “ana” or the user “raj”. Which filter do you type?
notes.back: A) `assignee:ana OR assignee:raj`
notes.choices:
A) `assignee:ana OR assignee:raj`
B) `assignee:ana assignee:raj`
C) `assignee:ana AND assignee:raj`
notes.choicesExplained: B: a space counts as `AND`. C: `AND` returns only issues where both statements are true.
notes.explanation: `OR` returns results where either statement is true.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Filtering and searching issues and pull requests”, “Using boolean operators”
notes.evidence: To return results where either statement is true, use `OR`.

notes.front: What are two things you can subscribe to notifications for?
notes.back: For example, the conversation in one issue, pull request or gist, and all activity in a repository (among others).
notes.explanation: The docs also list the status of automated workflows and a repository’s releases, security alerts or discussions.
notes.evidence: A conversation in a specific issue, pull request, or gist * All activity in a repository * CI activity, such as the status of workflows in repositories set up with GitHub Actions * Repository issues, pull requests, releases, security alerts, or discussions (if enabled)

notes.front: What are two actions that, in general, subscribe you to a conversation automatically?
notes.back: For example, opening the issue or pull request, and commenting on the thread (among others).
notes.explanation: The docs say “in general”, and also list being assigned, subscribing manually and having your username @mentioned.
notes.evidence: Been assigned to an issue or pull request. * Opened a pull request or issue. * Commented on a thread. * Subscribed to a thread manually by clicking **Watch** or **Subscribe**. * Had your username @mentioned.

notes.front: In your notifications inbox, how do you show only pull requests where someone requested your review?
notes.back: Filter by reason with the query reason:review-requested.
notes.explanation: The inbox labels each notification with the reason you received it, and you can filter on that reason.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About notifications”, “Reasons for receiving notifications”
notes.evidence: You can filter your inbox by the reason you're subscribed to notifications. For example, to only see pull requests where someone requested your review, you can use the `reason:review-requested` query filter.

notes.front: In the notifications inbox, marking a notification {{c1::Done}} removes it from the inbox.
notes.back: Done.
notes.explanation: Done notifications are not lost: you can review them together in the sidebar or with the query is:done.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About notifications”, “Triaging notifications from your inbox”
notes.evidence: Remove a notification from the inbox with **Done**. You can review **Done** notifications all in one place by clicking **Done** in the sidebar or by using the query `is:done`.

notes.front: How long does GitHub keep notifications that are not marked Saved?
notes.back: 3 months. Saved notifications are kept indefinitely.
notes.explanation: Saving is what exempts a notification from the 3-month limit.
notes.evidence: Notifications that are not marked as **Saved** are kept for 3 months. Notifications marked as **Saved** are kept indefinitely.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: You will need a notification about a design decision again in six months. What should you do with it in your inbox?
notes.back: B) Save it.
notes.choices:
A) Mark it Done
B) Save it
C) Mark it as read
notes.choicesExplained: A and C do not change how long it is kept; unsaved notifications are kept for only 3 months.
notes.explanation: Saved notifications are kept indefinitely, unsaved ones for 3 months.
notes.evidence: Notifications that are not marked as **Saved** are kept for 3 months. Notifications marked as **Saved** are kept indefinitely.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · GitHub Docs as of that date

notes.front: Is a secret gist private?
notes.back: No. It stays out of Discover and other people's searches, but anyone who has its web address can see it.
notes.explanation: Being hidden from listings is not the same as being protected: the link alone gives access.
notes.evidence: Secret gists aren't private. If you send the URL of a secret gist to a friend, they'll be able to see it. However, if someone you don't know discovers the URL, they'll also be able to see your gist.

notes.front: A developer must share some code with one colleague, and it must be kept away from anyone else. What does GitHub suggest?
notes.back: B) A private repository.
notes.choices:
A) A secret gist
B) A private repository
C) A public gist
notes.choicesExplained: A: a secret gist is not private; anyone with its link can see it. C: public gists are listed in Discover and searchable.
notes.explanation: The docs point people who need to keep code away from prying eyes to a private repository instead of a secret gist.
notes.evidence: Secret gists aren't private. If you send the URL of a secret gist to a friend, they'll be able to see it. However, if someone you don't know discovers the URL, they'll also be able to see your gist. If you need to keep your code away from prying eyes, you may want to create a private repository instead.

notes.front: After creating a gist, which way can you change its visibility?
notes.back: Only from secret to public. A public gist cannot be converted to secret.
notes.explanation: Making a secret gist public is done by editing it and updating its visibility.
notes.evidence: After creating a gist, you cannot convert it from public to secret. However, a secret gist can be made public by editing the gist and updating the visibility to public.

notes.front: Who can see the wiki of a private repository?
notes.back: Only people with access to the repository.
notes.explanation: A wiki follows its repository: in a public repository the wiki is public too.
notes.evidence: If you create a wiki in a public repository, the wiki is available to the public. If you create a wiki in a private repository, only people with access to the repository can access the wiki.

notes.front: When do search engines index a GitHub wiki?
notes.back: Only when it has 500 or more stars and is configured to prevent public editing.
notes.explanation: If you need search engines to index your content, the docs suggest GitHub Pages in a public repository.
notes.evidence: Search engines will only index wikis with 500 or more stars that you configure to prevent public editing. For more information, see [Changing access permissions for wikis](/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/changing-access-permissions-for-wikis). > > If you need search engines to index your content, you can use GitHub Pages in a public repository.

notes.front: What must the repository holding a user or organization GitHub Pages site be named?
notes.back: <owner>.github.io, where <owner> is the personal or organization account name.
notes.explanation: The site’s default address is the same name, http(s)://<owner>.github.io.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub Pages?”, “Types of GitHub Pages sites”
notes.evidence: Must be stored in a repository named <owner>.github.io, where <owner> is the personal or organization account name

notes.front: Where are the source files of a GitHub Pages project site kept?
notes.back: In a folder within the repository that holds the project’s code.
notes.explanation: A project site lives with its project, unlike a user or organization site, which needs its own specially named repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub Pages?”, “Types of GitHub Pages sites”
notes.evidence: Stored in a folder within the repository that contains the project

notes.front: How many GitHub Pages sites can you have: user or organization sites, and project sites?
notes.back: One user or organization site per account; one project site per repository.
notes.explanation: The two limits count different things: accounts for one type, repositories for the other.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub Pages?”, “Types of GitHub Pages sites”
notes.evidence: Maximum of one pages site per account

notes.front: You care about one bug report in a busy repository, but not the rest of its activity. What should you subscribe to?
notes.back: C) The conversation in that one issue.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: notifications cover only your own repositories
B) All activity in the repository
C) The conversation in that one issue
notes.choicesExplained: B would bring every update in the repository. A: you can subscribe to a conversation in a specific issue.
notes.explanation: Subscriptions can be as narrow as one issue’s conversation or as wide as all activity in a repository.
notes.evidence: A conversation in a specific issue, pull request, or gist * All activity in a repository

notes.front: The user “mira” wants a personal GitHub Pages site at the address mira.github.io. Where must its files go?
notes.back: B) A repository named mira.github.io.
notes.choices:
A) A folder in any of her project repositories
B) A repository named mira.github.io
C) Her profile README
notes.choicesExplained: B describes a project site, which is published under a path after mira.github.io. C is not a Pages source.
notes.explanation: User and organization sites must be stored in a repository named after the account, followed by .github.io.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “What is GitHub Pages?”, “Types of GitHub Pages sites”
notes.evidence: Must be stored in a repository named <owner>.github.io, where <owner> is the personal or organization account name

notes.front: A developer wants to share one short script with others, as something they could also clone. Which GitHub feature fits best?
notes.back: C) A gist.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Pages
B) A wiki
C) A gist
notes.choicesExplained: B holds long-form project documentation. C publishes a website.
notes.explanation: Gists are a simple way to share code snippets, and each one is a Git repository that can be cloned.
notes.evidence: Gists provide a simple way to share code snippets with others. Every gist is a Git repository, which means that it can be forked and cloned.

notes.front: A project’s README covers what it does. The team now wants long pages on how it was designed and its core principles, inside the repository. Which feature fits?
notes.back: A) The repository’s wiki.
notes.choices:
A) The repository’s wiki
B) A gist
C) A longer README
notes.choicesExplained: A is for sharing code snippets. C: the README is meant to tell quickly what the project can do.
notes.explanation: The wiki is for long-form content such as design and core principles, beyond what the README covers.
notes.evidence: You can use your repository's wiki to share long-form content about your project, such as how to use it, how you designed it, or its core principles. A README file quickly tells what your project can do, while you can use a wiki to provide additional documentation.

notes.front: A new open-source project needs documentation that search engines will index. It has few stars. What do the docs suggest?
notes.back: C) GitHub Pages in a public repository.
notes.choices:
A) A wiki
B) A secret gist
C) GitHub Pages in a public repository
notes.choicesExplained: A: search engines index only wikis with 500 or more stars that block public editing. B: secret gists do not show up in search.
notes.explanation: The wiki docs point to GitHub Pages when content must be indexed by search engines.
notes.evidence: Search engines will only index wikis with 500 or more stars that you configure to prevent public editing. For more information, see [Changing access permissions for wikis](/en/communities/documenting-your-project-with-wikis/changing-access-permissions-for-wikis). > > If you need search engines to index your content, you can use GitHub Pages in a public repository.
